approvedAsIs.name: Stinging nettle
reasons: No missing deadly lookalike. Both real killers for a nettle patch are present: white snakeroot (Ageratina altissima) east of the Rockies and poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) with water hemlock (Cicuta maculata / C. douglasii) folded into the same tell for the West/Northwest/Southwest. The range split is correct and stated explicitly ('west of the Great Plains, the plant below is your deadly one instead'), so a forager in either half of the country is pointed at the right threat. Contact-hazard neighbours (wild parsnip, giant hogweed, poison ivy) are covered in `parts` rather than padded into the lookalike list, which is the right placement.

The white snakeroot tell survives the season it is actually needed in. It refuses to use flowers (correctly noting bloom is Aug-Oct per Illinois Extension / July-Oct per Minnesota Wildflowers, i.e. useless in the spring shoot window) and gives four separators that all work on a young opposite-leaved plant: papery stipules 5-15 mm at every node vs. an aster with none anywhere; 3-nerved venation vs. one midrib with pinnate side veins; squarish bristly stem with stinging hairs on the veins beneath vs. terete and smooth; and the sting. It also explicitly kills two false tells - petiole length (they overlap) and 'coarsely toothed' (both are) - and warns that fine soft down is normal on snakeroot so hairs do not acquit it, only stinging bristles do.

The poison hemlock entry is framed with the correct risk model: not a leaf twin but the deadly plant standing in the nettle patch, on word-for-word nettle ground (nitrogen-loving, stream and ditch banks, riparian floodplain), with first-year rosettes green and up through the whole spring window. Tells are part-appropriate for a rosette (3-4x pinnately divided lacy leaves, ALTERNATE, hollow hairless purple-blotched stem, mousy smell) and it names the specific failure mode - Illinois Extension is explicit that hemlock does not burn skin, so nothing warns you at the moment of contact, and the danger is cutting a fistful of mixed greens rather than inspecting every stem.

The sting logic is stated asymmetrically and correctly, which is the single most important thing in a nettle entry: the sting proves stinging hairs, not edibility (Cnidoscolus stings harder and is not a potherb), and absence of sting is not a safety test because snakeroot and hemlock do not sting either. Tread-softly is separated by alternate palmately-lobed leaves and white latex vs. opposite simple leaves and clear sap. The wood nettle caveat is genuinely careful: Laportea's ALTERNATE leaves invert the opposite-leaf shortcut, so when hunting wood nettle the stipules and the sting have to carry the whole identification.

Required preparation is present and specific, not vague. Concrete durations for disarming the trichomes (60-90 second blanch, or two minutes covered steaming), with NC State's more conservative five-minute boil attributed alongside; an explicit 'do not eat intact raw leaves'; and stop harvesting at flower tassels for cystoliths. Contact protocol is specific too: sight-match before touching anything, confirm with the back of ONE fingertip on an already-matched leaf, never sweep a bare arm through mixed vegetation, then gloves, long sleeves and scissors. Contamination guidance (avoid manure/corral/over-fertilised ground because a 90-second blanch will not deal with faecal pathogens, plus the nitrate point) and the medical notes (warfarin/vitamin K, diuretics and antihypertensives, pregnancy, rare systemic IgE reaction) are appropriate for a plant people drink daily as tea.

Schema conforms exactly. caution 'expert' is right because deadly lookalikes exist; all six danger values are legal ('deadly','deadly','toxic','unpalatable','unpalatable','toxic'); all four terrain values are legal and match the habitat; every lookalike has name/danger/tell; all required fields present with no extras.

Months are correctly 0-indexed and consistent with the prose: [1,2,3,4,5,8,9] = Feb-Jun plus Sep-Oct, which matches 'opens late February into March in the maritime Northwest and low-elevation California... May into June on northern and high-elevation ground' and the second cutting in September and October. The fall window is safe as written because the entry notes white snakeroot is in full flower by then and can no longer hide in the patch.

NON-BLOCKING DEFECT TO FIX BEFORE PUBLISH - regions omits 'mountain'. In src/data/seasonal-regional.ts the 'mountain' id is labelled 'Mountain & Southwest' and covers MT, WY, CO, NM, AZ, UT, ID, NV, yet the entry's own habitat text says that in the Southwest nettle is strictly riparian and 'is the most abundant nettle in Arizona', and harvest says the window runs 'into July above 8,000 ft in the Rockies and Southwest'. Since ForageSection filters entries by region (forageByTerrain(region, month)), an Arizona or Colorado user never sees this entry at all. This fails safe - it hides the entry rather than sending anyone to the wrong place or time - so it does not block, but 'mountain' should be added (and 'southcentral' considered, given the entry itself flags Cnidoscolus texanus in Texas and Oklahoma; other entries in this file such as Common chickweed do list all six regions, so this is an inconsistency, not a house style).

Minor, cosmetic: with 'mountain' added, month 6 (July) would be worth including to match the entry's own 'into July above 8,000 ft in the Rockies and Southwest'. Harmless as-is because being out of the listed window carries no hazard for this species.

approvedAsIs.name: Wild garlic (field garlic)
reasons: No missing deadly lookalike. The set that actually kills or hospitalizes people who pick narrow-leaved bulb plants out of US lawns and pastures is all present and correctly ranked: death camas (Toxicoscordion venenosum / nuttallii / leimanthoides), fly poison (Amianthium muscitoxicum), star-of-Bethlehem (Ornithogalum umbellatum, correctly rated deadly on the cardiac-glycoside evidence even though NC State rates it only 'medium'), Narcissus, Galanthus/Leucojum, and Nothoscordum bivalve. I checked the plausible omissions - Convallaria, Colchicum, Muscari, Zephyranthes, Hyacinthus - and none is both deadly and a realistic confusion for a slender hollow-leaved Allium; all are caught by the tells already given.

caution: 'expert' is correct per src/data/foraging.ts (deadly lookalike exists), and three lookalikes carry danger: 'deadly', so ForageSection.tsx line 94 surfaces the warning on the collapsed row too.

Every tell works on the parts and in the season actually harvested. The primary discriminator is smell on a crushed leaf, which works on leaves in Oct-Jun and on dug bulbs. The structural backups are all leaf/bulb characters (solid vs hollow, keeled vs terete, black vs tan bulb tunic, white midvein), never flower characters. The entry explicitly flags that star-of-Bethlehem is leaf-only through the Feb-May window so no flower is available to help - exactly the failure mode I was looking for, and it is pre-empted rather than committed. The single flower-dependent tell (two bracts on Nothoscordum) is offered as a supplementary positive character for a lookalike rated merely unpalatable, not as the discriminator.

The smell test is not left as naive advice. It names the two real failure modes with a specific procedure for each: onion contamination on the fingers producing false positives (sourced to BfR), and the fistful-of-blades problem where field garlic interleaved with star-of-Bethlehem in the same square foot defeats per-plant testing. Instructions are specific, not vague: test with clean hands or tear a fresh leaf unhandled, cut/pick one plant at a time, sort and smell dug bulbs individually, and cut a leaf across NEAR THE BASE for the hollow/round check (correct - that is where A. vineale is reliably terete and hollow).

The A. vineale (round, hollow) vs A. canadense (flat, solid) distinction is handled correctly rather than conflated, and the entry closes the loop that most guides leave open: flat solid leaves that DO smell of onion means native wild onion, also edible - so a beginner who fails the shape check but passes the smell check is not left guessing. The blanket claim 'every dangerous plant listed above is flat or keeled and solid' holds for all six lookalikes.

Schema conforms exactly. All required fields present, no extras; caution, all six lookalikes[].danger, all three terrain values and all four region ids are valid enum members; months are integers 0-11. The 0-indexed months [0,1,2,3,4,5,9,10,11] correctly encode a winter-growing perennial (Oct-Jun green, summer-dormant), with May-Jun retained for the aerial bulbils - not an off-by-one.

No required safety preparation is omitted: A. vineale needs no cooking or leaching, and the one real ingestion caveat (sulfides causing nausea in large raw quantities, so treat as a seasoning) is stated. Contamination guidance is present and correctly targeted at herbicide-treated turf and dog-walking lawns, which is precisely where this plant is most abundant.

NOT BLOCKING, coverage gap worth fixing: regions omits 'southcentral' (TX, OK per REGIONS in src/data/seasonal-regional.ts). A. vineale is established in eastern Texas and Oklahoma, and the entry's own habitat text ('the whole eastern half of the country') and its death camas tell (T. nuttallii 'from Kansas and Oklahoma through ... Texas') both contradict the omission. The error direction is conservative - TX/OK users simply never see the entry via forageFor(), so nobody is sent anywhere unsafe - but they also lose the death camas warning for a region where T. nuttallii is a live risk. Adding 'southcentral' would be an improvement.

NOT BLOCKING, cosmetic: the first lookalike's name field carries the full three-species range breakdown (~200 chars). ForageSection.tsx line 96 joins deadly lookalike names untruncated into the collapsed-row 'Confusable with ...' line, so that row will run long. No information is lost; consider moving the range detail from name into tell.

NOT BLOCKING, presentation mismatch in the component rather than the data: the life-safety smell-test rule lives in the harvest field, which ForageSection.tsx line 108 labels 'Leave enough.' - a conservation heading. The text opens with a capitalised 'THE RULE FOR THIS WHOLE GENUS:' so it still reads unmistakably, and the field is only visible when the row is expanded. Worth a component-level fix, not an objection to this entry.

approvedAsIs.name: Chicken of the Woods
reasons: No deadly lookalike is missing. I swept the orange-bracket/oak-base niche for anything that could kill: Omphalotus illudens and Hapalopilus nidulans are both present with concrete tells; Gymnopilus junonius and Armillaria are explicitly disposed of by the gills+stalk test in the jack-o'-lantern tell; Phaeolus schweinitzii and other conifer brackets fall to the absolute conifer-substrate rule; Bondarzewia and Meripilus are edible. Extension consensus (MDC, UF/IFAS, Cornell) is that this species has no deadly lookalike, so caution 'care' is the correct level and is internally consistent with all five lookalikes being danger 'toxic' (no 'deadly' entry that would force 'expert').

The real hazards for this species are not lookalikes, and all are covered: raw/undercooked GI distress, individual sensitivity (~10% severe reactions per the Cornell blog, including onset after years of uneventful eating), a mandatory small test portion with a one-day wait, hardwood-hosts-only with yew called out as the hardest no, and black locust flagged as unsettled caution rather than asserted fact.

Every tell works on the part and at the time it is actually harvested — pore surface vs true gills on a stalk, two-tone bright orange over sulfur-yellow vs uniform cinnamon, host wood, and instant KOH violet on Hapalopilus. None depends on a feature absent from a fresh bracket. Bioluminescence on the jack-o'-lantern is correctly hedged as secondary rather than load-bearing, and the Gulf tell explicitly blocks the dangerous inference 'white pores, therefore L. cincinnatus' by anchoring on shelf-on-trunk vs rosette-from-soil.

Schema is satisfied exactly: all required ForageSpecies fields present with correct types and no extras; caution 'care' is a valid Caution; all lookalikes[].danger are the valid literal 'toxic'; terrain values woodland/edge/disturbed are valid Terrain members; regions northeast/southeast/midwest are valid RegionIds.

Months [4,5,6,7,8,9,10] are correct 0-indexed May-November, matching the entry's own cited sources (MDC May-November in Missouri, UMass July-October in southern New England). No risk of sending someone out in a dead season, and the early-season edge is before jack-o'-lantern fruits.

Regions correctly enforce the two range limits as safety limits: mountain and west are excluded because no true L. sulphureus occurs west of the Rockies, and southcentral (TX/OK) is omitted conservatively, which fails safe by simply not surfacing the entry.

Harvest guidance is sound and includes a real physical-safety warning most guides omit: this is a brown rot that structurally weakens the trunk, so do not climb and do not work under a colonised trunk in wind — take from the ground or leave it.

NON-BLOCKING: 'Cook it thoroughly' gives no duration, and undercooking is the most common cause of illness with this species. Mitigated by the mandatory small test portion plus one-day wait, but a concrete floor (cook through roughly 15-20 minutes, no rare centers) would be better.

NON-BLOCKING: region 'southeast' spans NC/SC/GA/FL/AL/MS/TN/KY/AR/LA, so it includes the Gulf rim that the habitat text says is out of scope. The caveat and the gilbertsonii lookalike are both present, but the range limit sits deep in the habitat paragraph while lead() surfaces only the opening sentence in the collapsed row — worth hoisting into the first sentence or the indicator. Dropping 'southeast' would be worse, since it would strip the entry from the Carolinas, Georgia and Tennessee where true L. sulphureus is common.

NON-BLOCKING judgment call: Hapalopilus nidulans is classed 'toxic' rather than 'deadly'. Defensible — the published cases including the cited PubMed 23937526 involved severe CNS and renal injury but recovery with supportive care, with no confirmed fatality — and the KOH-violet tell is decisive. Flagging it because reclassifying it as 'deadly' would force caution to 'expert'.

approvedAsIs.name: Hen of the Woods (Maitake)
reasons: No deadly lookalike is missing, so caution 'care' is correct. Grifola frondosa has no deadly lookalike in the US literature: the confusables are all pored polypores that are edible (Meripilus sumstinei, Bondarzewia berkeleyi, Polyporus umbellatus) or merely inedible (Phaeolus schweinitzii), plus jack-o'-lantern, which MDC explicitly describes as making you 'very sick for a few days' but 'not life-threatening' — correctly coded 'toxic', not 'deadly'.

The destroying angel / death cap risk is handled the right way. They are mycorrhizal with oak and fruit within feet of a hen in the same weeks, but they are not lookalikes for a pored rosette. The entry flags them in habitat prose with a hard bagging rule ('nothing white, gilled and stalked should ever ride home in the same bag') instead of listing them as lookalikes, which would have wrongly forced caution to 'expert' and diluted that flag for entries that genuinely have one.

Every checkable numeric claim verifies exactly against the cited sources. MushroomExpert confirms Meripilus at '6-8 round to angular pores per mm', caps 5-20 cm (entry: 2-8 in.), and Grifola at '1-3 angular... pores per mm', 'not bruising', 'lavender gray when young... staining yellowish' — matching the entry's 'never blackens, it only yellows with age'. MDC confirms jack-o'-lantern July-October, clusters from buried wood, gills 'sharp-edged; crowded... descend the stalk'; and Berkeley's at 3-12 in. cream caps with 'Pores wide, angular' on oaks, edible young.

The tells work on the part and in the season actually harvested. All four keys are readable on the fresh fruiting body in hand at any age: gills-vs-pores plus orange flesh for jack-o'-lantern, instant black bruising for Meripilus, cream colour plus few large caps for Bondarzewia, brown corky flesh plus bruising pores for Phaeolus. None depends on a feature absent at harvest time.

The host-tree trap is explicitly pre-empted — the Phaeolus tell states the conifer host is 'corroboration, not proof - identify it by the brown flesh and the bruising', and the Berkeley's tell warns 'Go by the cream-white colour and the small number of big caps, not by size alone', which is necessary because Kuo gives hen caps up to 14 cm, overlapping Berkeley's 3-12 in. range at the low end.

Months [7,8,9,10] = August-November, matching the stated 'late August into November' season with a mid-September to early October peak, and the early-season risk is self-flagged: an August hen overlaps peak Meripilus and Phaeolus season, so the entry tells you to run the checks properly that early.

Regions northeast/midwest/southeast are correct. Missouri falls in 'midwest' in this schema, so the MDC sourcing is covered; southcentral (TX/OK) is correctly excluded on 3 Texas GBIF records; mountain and west are correctly excluded since Kuo places the species east of the Rockies. Any under-inclusion here is a 'you won't find it' error, not a safety error.

Schema validates: all required ForageSpecies fields present with no extras, caution and all lookalike danger values legal, terrain and regions within the allowed enums, and months 0-indexed within 0-11.

Safety preparation is unusually complete — never eat raw, reject soft/sour-smelling/larvae-riddled clumps (correctly identified as the actual leading cause of illness with this species), modest first portion, allergy note, plus the hypoglycemic-drug and warfarin/INR interactions sourced to Memorial Sloan Kettering.

NON-BLOCKING: 'cook it thoroughly, a slow simmer or roast' gives no minimum time. Maitake has no defined thermolabile toxin requiring a fixed protocol, so this is not a required-duration case, but a stated floor (e.g. at least 15-20 minutes) would serve a beginner better.

NON-BLOCKING, the one gap worth closing: habitat explicitly includes 'parks, yards and old fencerows' and terrain includes 'disturbed', but there is no warning about chemically treated lawns, street and park trees, or contaminated urban soil. The hazard is chronic rather than acute, so it does not block, but a line advising against oaks in treated turf or roadside plantings should be added.

NON-BLOCKING, cosmetic: terrain 'upland' (defined as dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub) is a stretch for a species that needs large mature oaks, though defensible for oak-hickory ridges. Also, hen pores are called 'visibly angular (1-3 per mm)' against Meripilus but 'fine and whitish' against Bondarzewia — both correct as relative comparisons and both matching the sources, but a reader taking 'fine' and 'coarse' as absolutes could be briefly confused. Polyporus umbellatus, the other lookalike Kuo names, is absent, but it is edible and choice, so there is no safety consequence.

approvedRevisedEntries.name: Common blue violet
approvedRevisedEntries.habitat: Lawns, verges, parks and the shaded strip where mown grass runs out under trees; rich moist woods and woodland edges; old fields; stream banks and swamp margins (Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center gives the habitat as rich moist woods and swamps, NC State adds streambeds). Native across the East and Midwest, reaching its southwestern limit in eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas - it is not a desert Southwest plant, and the stemless blue violets of the Rockies and Pacific states are a different complex not covered here. Wherever it grows it grows mixed in with other low spring rosettes: harmless ones like garlic mustard, toxic ones like lesser celandine, buttercup and ground ivy, and - in old plantings, cemeteries, homestead yards and the shaded edge of an old lawn - dense colonies of lily-of-the-valley, which is deadly. That mixing, not the violet itself, is the whole problem - which is why leaf-only identification is a bad habit here.
approvedRevisedEntries.indicator: Damp, rich, shaded ground under maple, ash or oak - the mossy strip where a mown lawn gives out beneath the trees is the reliable spot. Read that strip as a warning as well as a signal: beside an old house it is also exactly where lily-of-the-valley was planted a century ago and never left, so expect to find both on the same few square feet.
approvedRevisedEntries.parts: Leaves and flowers only, and only from stemless blue- or white-flowered violets. Young heart-shaped leaves raw in salad or cooked as a mild, slightly mucilaginous green (a decent soup thickener); flowers candied, made into jelly, syrup or violet vinegar, or scattered raw over a salad. The leaves and flowers carry saponins, so treat them as a salad component or potherb in normal portions rather than a bulk green - large helpings can cause nausea, cramping or a laxative effect. Roots, rhizomes and seeds are NOT food: they concentrate the saponins and are strongly emetic and purgative (Illinois Extension: 'Both the flowers and leaves of common blue violet are edible, but the roots are not'). Seed capsules ripen inside the harvest window, so keep them out of the basket. African violet is an unrelated houseplant and is not food.

lookalikes.name: Lily-of-the-valley - European (Convallaria majalis) and the native Appalachian species (C. pseudomajalis, syn. C. majuscula)
lookalikes.tell: The one that can kill you, and it is a leaf-season problem: Convallaria leaves push up in March-April, a month or more ahead of its own May bells, so through most of this entry's Feb-June leaf window there is nothing but foliage to judge it on. Judge it leaf by leaf, on four features, every one of them visible without a flower. (1) VEINS - the single most reliable check, and it works on one detached leaf: a violet leaf is palmately veined, the main veins fanning out from the point where the stalk meets the blade at the notch of the heart and branching into a net; a Convallaria leaf is parallel-veined like the monocot it is, unbranched veins running the length of the blade and converging at the tip. (2) BLADE SHAPE AND MARGIN: violet blades are heart-shaped, broadest near the base, with scalloped, round-toothed margins the whole way round; Convallaria blades are elliptic to oblanceolate, roughly 4-8 in long, broadest at or above the middle, tapering to a point, with a completely smooth, entire margin. (3) HOW IT MEETS THE GROUND: every violet leaf stands alone on its own bare round petiole rising straight from a ground-level crown; Convallaria carries two, sometimes three, leaves per shoot whose tapered bases wrap and sheathe one another into one shared stalk. Two leaves sharing a sheathed base means it is not a violet - stop there. (4) UNDERGROUND: a violet has one stout knobby rhizome with plain fibrous roots and stays a discrete clump; Convallaria runs on a slender creeping horizontal rhizome with roots along its length and forms a dense unbroken colony that pushes shoots up between the violets, not politely to one side. Two things that do NOT work here. Smell is worthless: the torn-leaf onion test that separates this plant from ramps proves nothing in a violet patch, because violet leaves have no smell either. And early season is the worst season: in March a Convallaria shoot is still furled into a narrow upright spear and has not opened out to show its shape, so wait for the blade to unroll before you judge it. Habitat overlaps exactly - C. majalis persists and spreads for decades in old plantings, cemeteries, homestead yards and shaded lawn edges, the same mown-grass-to-tree strip this entry sends you to, and NC State puts the native C. pseudomajalis in mountain hardwood forest and rocky woodland at roughly 3,000-5,000 ft from northern Virginia and West Virginia south to northern Georgia. Every part is toxic, leaves and berries alike, and so is the water from a vase: cardiac glycosides (convallatoxin among dozens), rated high poison severity by NC State - burning mouth and throat, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, slow or irregular pulse, dilated pupils, headache, confusion, low blood pressure, and in severe cases seizures or coma. Treat any suspected ingestion as an emergency: call Poison Control on 1-800-222-1222 immediately, do not wait to see whether symptoms develop.

lookalikes.name: Lesser celandine / fig buttercup (Ficaria verna, syn. Ranunculus ficaria)
lookalikes.tell: The mistake that matters, because it happens before either plant flowers. Two structural tells, both checkable without a flower. (1) Leaf margin: violet leaves are toothed around the entire edge; celandine leaves are kidney-shaped with smooth, or at most gently lobed and wavy, margins (Penn State Extension makes this the primary separation). Do not use gloss - violet leaves are often waxy and shiny too, which is why lawn herbicides run off them. (2) Rootstock and growth form: pull one up. Celandine sits on a cluster of detachable pale fig-shaped tubers the size of a fingernail, often with small bulbils in the leaf axils later in the season, and it spreads as a dense unbroken carpet. A violet has one stout knobby rhizome with plain fibrous roots, no tubers, and grows as a discrete clump with each leaf on its own stalk. In flower it is trivial: celandine has about 8 glossy yellow petals; violet has 5 blue-purple petals, bilaterally symmetrical, with a nectar spur on the lower petal. NC State lists leaves, stems, roots and sap as poisonous (protoanemonin; vomiting, diarrhea, oral ulcers), and the sap can irritate skin.

lookalikes.name: Wild ginger (Asarum canadense) and the southeastern heartleafs (Hexastylis / Asarum arifolia group)
lookalikes.tell: The woodland-floor confusion rather than the lawn one - same shaded, moist, rich ground, same season, also heart-shaped. Use the margin first: every wild ginger and heartleaf has an ENTIRE, untoothed leaf edge, and its leaf is thick and leathery; a violet leaf is thinner and scallop-toothed all the way round. Then use the plant: A. canadense carries a pair of dull gray-green, softly hairy, conspicuously veined leaves 3-6 in across from the tip of one short stalk, and dies back for winter; the southeastern heartleafs are EVERGREEN, glossy, leathery, often silver-mottled, and their leaves rise singly from creeping underground stems (NC State, Hexastylis arifolia) - so the 'leaves in pairs' rule you may have read is useless south of Virginia. Scratch the rhizome or stem: a ginger-to-peppery smell means put it down; a faint or absent smell proves nothing, so never clear a plant on scent alone. Its flower is a single brownish-purple cup sitting in the leaf litter under the leaves, easily missed - so a wild ginger can look 'flowerless' in a patch of blooming violets. Do not eat any part: NC State rates leaves, stems and roots poisonous for aristolochic acid, which is nephrotoxic and a carcinogen, with FDA warnings behind it. The damage is cumulative, delayed and silent, so 'I ate some and felt fine' means nothing here.

lookalikes.name: Kidneyleaf, creeping and bulbous buttercup (Ranunculus abortivus, R. repens, R. bulbosus)
lookalikes.tell: The most abundant kidney-shaped basal leaf in the same lawns, verges and moist woods. R. abortivus basal leaves are round to heart or kidney-shaped with scalloped margins on long stalks (UMass Weed Herbarium) - genuinely violet-like at a glance. The give-away is that a buttercup builds an upright, branching, LEAFY flowering stem, and the leaves on that stem are deeply cut into 3-5 narrow lobes, nothing like the basal ones; R. repens goes further and divides its leaves into three stalked leaflets, often pale-blotched, and runs on above-ground stolons. A violet never makes a leafy stem at all: leaves and flower stalks each rise separately, bare, from a ground-level crown. Flowers are small, glossy, 5-petalled and yellow. All Ranunculus carry ranunculin, which becomes protoanemonin when the plant is crushed or chewed - a vesicant that blisters lips, mouth and gut and irritates skin (Cornell Poisonous Plants; Illinois Extension).

lookalikes.name: Marsh marigold (Caltha palustris)
lookalikes.tell: Do not separate these by wetness - blue violets grow on stream banks, seeps and swamp margins, and marsh blue violet (V. cucullata) grows right alongside marsh marigold. Separate them by structure. Marsh marigold builds thick, hairless, HOLLOW, branching stems that carry glossy leaves and flowers well above the ground, with leaves 3-6 in across; a violet is stemless, every leaf and every flower stalk rising individually from the crown, and no violet part is hollow. Flowers are 1-2 in across with 5-9 shiny waxy yellow sepals, versus a violet's 5 purple petals with a spur. Protoanemonin again; NC State is explicit that no part of this plant should ever be eaten raw.

lookalikes.name: Ground ivy / creeping Charlie (Glechoma hederacea)
lookalikes.tell: The commonest thing actually picked by mistake in a lawn. Roll the stem between your fingers: ground ivy stems are SQUARE, creep flat along the ground and root at every node, forming continuous runners, with pairs of opposite round-to-kidney leaves 0.5-1.5 in wide, scalloped, strongly minty-aromatic when crushed (WSU Hortsense). Violet leaves are alternate-looking only because each has its own bare stalk from a central crown - no runners, no square stems, no smell. Its flowers are small, two-lipped, tubular and blue-violet, clustered in the leaf axils along the runner, not solitary 5-petalled spurred flowers on bare stalks. Widely eaten historically as a pot herb, but its oil contains pulegone (the pennyroyal compound); it is regarded as toxic to livestock and is not something to eat by the handful or in pregnancy.

lookalikes.name: Yellow-flowered violets (e.g. downy yellow violet, Viola pubescens)
lookalikes.tell: Real violets, not poisonous, but they are caulescent: 1-2 leafy, hairy above-ground stems 4-10 in tall carry alternate leaves as well as any basal ones, and the flowers are yellow with brownish-purple veins on the lowest petal (NC State). NC State notes the flowers are edible only in limited quantities because they can have a laxative effect. Stick to the stemless blue- and white-flowered kinds, where every leaf and flower stalk rises straight from the ground.

approvedRevisedEntries.harvest: Confirm every plant in flower, and confirm it per plant, not per patch - then, for leaves, confirm every single leaf as well. The confusables here are separable at a glance once a violet flower is on the crown you are picking from - 5 blue-purple petals, bilaterally symmetrical, a spur on the lower petal, on a bare stalk from the base - and are genuinely easy to mix up before that. This is UMN Extension's advice too: beginning foragers should take flowers only, because violet leaves are easily confused with other non-edible plants. So take flowers freely from plants you can see blooming; take leaves only from a clump you personally watched flower, and pick leaf by leaf from that crown rather than stripping a handful out of mixed groundcover. But understand what the flower rule does not cover. A violet flower on the crown does NOT clear the leaves around it, and it cannot reach the deadly one at all: lily-of-the-valley puts its leaves up in March-April, ahead of its own May bells, so for most of this Feb-June leaf window it is standing there as foliage only, and in old plantings, cemeteries, homestead yards and shaded lawn edges it carpets the exact ground violets carpet, alongside celandine and buttercup. So run this test on every leaf, held in your hand, before it goes in the basket: the blade must be heart-shaped, scallop-toothed the whole way round, with veins fanning out from the notch and branching into a net, on its own single bare stalk. Any leaf that is smooth-edged, elliptic, tapered to a point, veined with unbranched lines running lengthwise, or that shares a sheathed base with a second leaf, is not a violet - discard the entire handful, not just that leaf, and start again from a crown you have re-checked. If you find lily-of-the-valley anywhere in the colony, take no leaves from that ground at all: take flowers only there, or move to a different patch, because its running rhizome pushes shoots up between the violet crowns rather than politely to one side. In March, wait for a furled shoot to unroll before judging it - a furled Convallaria spear has not yet shown its blade shape. Sort the whole harvest a second time at home, one leaf at a time on a flat surface, before it goes anywhere near a pan. Wild ginger and heartleaf hide their flowers in the litter, so an unflowering neighbour proves nothing. No roots, no rhizomes, no seed capsules. Keep portions moderate: the saponins make a big bowl of leaves a bad idea even when the identification is perfect. Sustainability: common and resilient, but pick flowers sparingly from any one patch, take only a few leaves per plant so the crown keeps producing, and leave plenty of bloom - fritillary butterfly caterpillars depend on violets. The bigger risk is chemical, not botanical: violets are most abundant in lawns, verges and parks, which are precisely the places sprayed for them - UMN's turf guidance recommends triclopyr, 2,4-D, dicamba and others against this exact species. Harvest only from ground whose treatment history you know.

reasons: SCHEMA: valid. All required fields present, no extras beyond optional `indicator`. caution/danger/terrain/region values all in-enum. months [1,2,3,4,5] are correctly 0-indexed = Feb-Jun, and the prose says "Feb-June" in three places — no off-by-one. Seven well-formed lookalikes, 22 sourced URLs.

DEADLY LOOKALIKE: present and correct. Convallaria (both C. majalis and the native C. pseudomajalis) is listed deadly, driving caution=expert. Its tell is substantively identical to the already-approved Ramps entry — same nomenclature incl. the syn. C. majuscula, same sheathed-2-3-leaves-per-shoot structure, same creeping-rhizome habit, same NC State cardiac-glycoside toxicology and 3,000-5,000 ft Appalachian range. No contradiction introduced into the corpus.

OUT-OF-SEASON TELL — the check this entry most had to pass, and it passes. It states outright that Convallaria foliage is up in March-April, a month ahead of its own May bells, so for most of the Feb-Jun leaf window the flower-confirmation rule cannot reach the deadly one at all, and it supplies four flower-independent tells (palmate net venation vs parallel unbranched; crenate cordate vs entire elliptic; single bare petiole vs sheathed pair; clumping knobby rhizome vs running colonial rhizome).

It also actively disarms two traps rather than leaving them latent: it says the torn-leaf onion test is worthless here because violets are scentless too (a forager carrying the rule over from the Ramps entry would otherwise be badly misled), and it says a furled March Convallaria spear has not yet shown its blade shape so wait for it to unroll. Same discipline on the celandine gloss tell and on the "wild ginger leaves come in pairs" rule, which it correctly says fails south of Virginia for evergreen Hexastylis.

HARVEST PROTOCOL is positive-ID and failure-safe, not a list of negatives: every leaf must be held in hand and pass all four criteria before it enters the basket; one failure discards the whole handful, not just that leaf; a second one-at-a-time sort at home; no leaf harvest at all from any colony containing Convallaria (correctly justified by its rhizome pushing shoots up between the violet crowns, not politely to one side). The positive test also catches unlisted confusables — any monocot (Colchicum, Narcissus) fails the venation criterion.

PARTS/PREPARATION is complete: roots, rhizomes and seed capsules excluded as emetic/purgative, with the specific note that capsules ripen inside the harvest window; saponin portion limit stated for leaves and flowers; yellow caulescent violets excluded; African violet disclaimed. It also flags the hazard that actually bites lawn foragers — UMN recommends triclopyr, 2,4-D and dicamba against this exact species in turf, so harvest only from ground whose spray history you know.

DANGER TIERS match published calibration: Glechoma unpalatable, wild ginger / lesser celandine / kidneyleaf buttercup toxic — the same tiers the approved Garlic mustard entry uses for the same four plants.

COSMETIC — regions omits `southcentral` while the habitat text explicitly says the plant reaches eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas. Under-claiming range is the safe direction, but a southcentral user won't be shown the entry; either add the region or drop the OK/TX sentence.

COSMETIC — no size is given for the violet's own leaf (~1-4 in wide) although sizes are given for Convallaria (4-8 in), A. canadense (3-6 in) and Caltha (3-6 in), so those contrasts are only half-usable. Relatedly, Convallaria leaf length reads "roughly 4-8 in" here vs "6-14 in long, 2-5 in wide" in the approved Ramps entry; different species in each and size is load-bearing in neither, but the two entries will look like they disagree.

COSMETIC — two woodland-floor plants sharing the entry's own "each leaf alone on its own bare stalk from a ground-level crown" architecture are unlisted: bloodroot (Sanguinaria canadensis, sanguinarine, orange-red sap) and Italian arum (Arum italicum, calcium oxalate, naturalised in exactly the old-planting and shaded-lawn-edge ground this entry sends people to, leaves present all spring). Both fail the required scalloped-margin/heart-shape criteria so the protocol already discards them; adding them would be cheap insurance.
